title: Battle of Britain
wiki_lead:
The Battle of Britain (German: Luftschlacht um England, lit. 'air battle for England') was a military campaign of the Second World War, in which the Royal Air Force (RAF) and the Fleet Air Arm (FAA) of the Royal Navy defended the United Kingdom against large-scale attacks by Nazi Germany's air force, the Luftwaffe. It was the first major military campaign fought entirely by air forces. It takes its name from the speech given by Prime Minister Winston Churchill to the House of Commons on 18 June 1940: "What General Weygand called the 'Battle of France' is over. I expect that the Battle of Britain is about to begin."
The Germans had rapidly overwhelmed France and the Low Countries in the Battle of France, leaving Britain to face the threat of invasion by sea. The German high command recognised the difficulties of a seaborne attack while the Royal Navy controlled the English Channel and the North Sea. The primary objective of the German forces was to compel Britain to agree to a negotiated peace settlement.
The British officially recognise the battle's duration as being from 10 July until 31 October 1940, which overlaps the period of large-scale night attacks known as the Blitz, that lasted from 7 September 1940 to 11 May 1941. German historians do not follow this subdivision and regard the battle as a single campaign lasting from July 1940 to May 1941, including the Blitz.
In July 1940, the air and sea blockade began, with the Luftwaffe mainly targeting coastal-shipping convoys, as well as ports and shipping centres such as Portsmouth. On 16 July, Hitler ordered the preparation of Operation Sea Lion as a potential amphibious and airborne assault on Britain, to follow once the Luftwaffe had air superiority over the Channel. On 1 August, the Luftwaffe was directed to achieve air superiority over the RAF, with the aim of incapacitating RAF Fighter Command; 12 days later, it shifted the attacks to RAF airfields and infrastructure. As the battle progressed, the Luftwaffe also targeted factories involved in aircraft production and strategic infrastructure. Eventually, it employed terror bombing on areas of political significance and on civilians. In September, RAF Bomber Command night raids disrupted the German preparation of converted barges, and the Luftwaffe's failure to overwhelm the RAF forced Hitler to postpone and eventually cancel Operation Sea Lion. The Luftwaffe proved unable to sustain daylight raids, but their continued night-bombing operations on Britain became known as the Blitz.
Germany's failure to destroy Britain's air defences and force it out of the conflict was the first major German defeat in the Second World War.

grok_lead: The Battle of Britain was a pivotal air campaign fought between the Royal Air Force (RAF) of the United Kingdom and the German Luftwaffe during the Second World War, taking place primarily over southern England from July 10 to October 31, 1940. It marked the first major military engagement conducted entirely by air forces and represented Nazi Germany's initial significant defeat, as the RAF successfully thwarted Luftwaffe efforts to achieve air superiority necessary for Operation Sea Lion, the planned invasion of Britain. Following the fall of France in June 1940, the campaign arose from Adolf Hitler's Directive No. 16, which aimed to force Britain to negotiate peace by bombing strategic targets, including airfields, radar stations, and later cities, in a bid to break RAF resistance and civilian morale. Under the leadership of Air Chief Marshal Sir Hugh Dowding, commander of RAF Fighter Command, British defenses relied on the innovative Dowding System, an integrated network of radar early warning, command centers, and observer corps that enabled efficient interception of incoming raids. The RAF deployed around 3,000 aircrew, supported by approximately 30,000 ground personnel, flying primarily Supermarine Spitfire and Hawker Hurricane fighters, while the Luftwaffe committed over 2,500 aircraft, including Messerschmitt Bf 109 fighters and Junkers Ju 87 Stuka dive bombers, under the direction of Reichsmarschall Hermann GÃ¶ring. The battle unfolded in phases: initial attacks on Channel shipping (the Kanalkampf), escalation to RAF infrastructure in August (Adlerangriff, or Eagle Attack), and a shift to night bombing of London in September after a Luftwaffe navigational error prompted retaliatory British raids on Berlin. Casualties were heavy on both sides, with the RAF losing 544 pilots killedâroughly one in six of those engagedâand 312 ground personnel, alongside the destruction of about 1,023 aircraft; the Luftwaffe suffered around 2,500 aircrew fatalities and the loss of approximately 1,887 aircraft. Notably, the campaign featured significant contributions from international volunteers, including over 140 Polish pilots who claimed 203.5 enemy aircraft destroyed, highlighting the multinational composition of the "Few," as Prime Minister Winston Churchill famously described the RAF defenders in his August 20, 1940, speech to Parliament. The RAF's resilience, bolstered by production rates that outpaced lossesâmanufacturing 498 new fighters in July aloneâproved decisive. The victory not only secured Britain's survival as a base for future Allied operations but also boosted national morale and demonstrated the effectiveness of defensive air power, influencing subsequent wartime strategies and earning enduring commemoration, such as Battle of Britain Day on September 15.
